Since you already enjoy **Adobe Premiere Pro** and have been learning **Lumetri Color, curves, and color wheels**, I’d focus on resources that combine editing fundamentals with Premiere-specific workflows.

### Free online resources

- **Adobe Premiere Pro Learn & Support**  
  Adobe’s official tutorials cover the interface, editing, audio, effects, color, captions, and exporting. Good for building a reliable foundation.  
  https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere-pro/tutorials.html

- **Adobe Video & Motion channel**  
  Useful demonstrations from Adobe experts, including new Premiere features and practical workflows.

- **Premiere Gal**  
  Clear, approachable tutorials on Premiere Pro, editing techniques, audio cleanup, color correction, and workflow improvements.  
  https://www.youtube.com/@PremiereGal

- **Justin Odisho**  
  Particularly helpful for learning effects, transitions, shortcuts, masking, adjustment layers, and efficient Premiere workflows.  
  https://www.youtube.com/@JustinOdisho

- **Cinecom.net**  
  Good for creative editing ideas, visual effects, transitions, and practical production techniques. Treat the more stylized tutorials as inspiration rather than essential fundamentals.

- **This Guy Edits**  
  Excellent for understanding the *reasoning* behind an edit—pacing, performance, emotion, and storytelling—not just which buttons to press.  
  https://www.youtube.com/@ThisGuyEdits

- **Frame.io Insider**  
  Strong articles and videos on editing theory, post-production workflows, collaboration, and professional practices.  
  https://blog.frame.io/

### Structured courses

- **LinkedIn Learning – Premiere Pro Essential Training**  
  A good guided path if you prefer lessons arranged from beginner through intermediate level.

- **Ripple Training**  
  Offers detailed Premiere Pro courses, including editing, audio, color, and professional workflows.  
  https://www.rippletraining.com/

- **Skillshare or Udemy**  
  These can be useful, but choose courses with recent reviews and versions compatible with your edition of Premiere. Look for courses that teach organization, storytelling, audio, and color—not just flashy transitions.

### Books worth reading

- **_In the Blink of an Eye_ — Walter Murch**  
  A short, influential book about why cuts work and how editing affects emotion and attention.

- **_The Grammar of the Edit_ — Christopher J. Bowen**  
  A practical introduction to continuity, pacing, shot selection, and editing structure.

- **_The Technique of Film Editing_ — Karel Reisz and Gavin Millar**  
  More historical and theoretical, but valuable for understanding how editing developed as a storytelling art.

### A practical learning path

1. Learn project organization, bins, sequences, codecs, and proxies.  
2. Practice basic cuts, continuity, pacing, and J-cuts/L-cuts.  
3. Improve dialogue editing and audio mixing.  
4. Learn color correction before creative grading—exposure, white balance, contrast, and skin tones first.  
5. Use Lumetri’s Creative panel and curves to establish a look only after the footage is balanced.  
6. Study edits from films, documentaries, music videos, or creators you admire.  
7. Complete small projects rather than watching tutorials indefinitely.

For practice, try editing the same short footage three ways: a fast-paced montage, a calm cinematic sequence, and a dialogue-focused scene. That will reinforce both the storytelling principles you’re learning and the Lumetri color-grading skills you’ve already been exploring.

Given your **Sony A7R IV, 24–70mm f/2.8 lens, Godox V1, and Gitzo GT3543LS**, I’d prioritize accessories that improve power, stability, flash control, and protection:

### Most useful additions

- **Extra Sony NP-FZ100 batteries**  
  Carry two or three genuine batteries, plus a dual charger. The A7R IV can charge over USB-C, but a dedicated charger is more convenient when traveling.

- **Fast, reliable SD cards**  
  Use UHS-II V60 or V90 cards from reputable brands, ideally two cards so you can use the A7R IV’s dual slots for backup. Carry a spare rather than relying on one high-capacity card.

- **L-bracket or Arca-Swiss plate**  
  A camera-specific L-bracket will make switching between landscape and portrait orientation much easier on your Gitzo tripod. Check that it leaves access to the camera’s ports and battery door.

- **Quality tripod head**  
  The GT3543LS legs are only half of a tripod system. A sturdy **ball head** is versatile for general photography; a **three-way or geared head** is better for careful product and landscape composition.

- **82mm circular polarizer**  
  Your 24–70mm f/2.8 lens likely uses an 82mm filter thread. A good polarizer can reduce reflections on foliage, glass, and water and deepen skies. Consider an 82mm filter plus step-up rings for any smaller lenses you add later.

- **Lens hood and protective filter**  
  Use the manufacturer’s hood and, if you want front-element protection, a high-quality, multicoated clear or UV filter. Avoid inexpensive filters that can reduce contrast or create flare.

### For the Godox V1

- **Godox magnetic accessory kit**  
  A diffuser dome, bounce card, grid, and colored gels can give you more control for both event photography and your candle product shots.

- **Compact light stand and umbrella/softbox**  
  A small stand with a collapsible white shoot-through umbrella or softbox will produce much softer light than mounting the V1 directly on the camera.

- **Godox XPro II-S or X2T-S transmitter**  
  If you want to use the V1 off-camera, a Sony-compatible Godox trigger will provide wireless TTL and manual control. The transmitter is especially useful for product photography.

- **Spare V1 battery and charger**  
  A second battery is valuable during longer shoots or markets where flash use is frequent.

### Travel and handling

- **Comfortable camera strap or sling**  
  Since you were considering a more comfortable Sony-oriented camera bag, look for a strap with a quick-adjust system and a secure attachment method. A sling can be more convenient than a backpack for the 24–70mm setup.

- **Rain cover and microfiber kit**  
  Add a camera rain cover, rocket blower, lens brush, and clean microfiber cloths. Use a blower before wiping the lens to avoid dragging grit across the coating.

- **Cable release or Sony-compatible remote**  
  Useful for tripod landscapes, long exposures, and self-portraits. The A7R IV also supports remote control through Sony’s mobile app.

- **USB-C power bank**  
  A high-capacity USB-C PD power bank can recharge the camera and other devices while traveling. Use one with adequate output and a short, durable USB-C cable.

### My suggested buying order

1. Extra batteries and UHS-II cards  
2. L-bracket and a quality tripod head  
3. Off-camera Godox trigger, stand, and softbox  
4. Polarizer and protective filter  
5. Rain protection, strap, and cleaning accessories  

For your candle photography, the **off-camera trigger, softbox, and polarizer** would likely make the biggest practical difference; for landscapes and your Grand Teton trip, prioritize the **L-bracket, tripod head, spare batteries, and weather protection**.

Given your focus on **deep learning for medical image analysis—especially segmentation, multimodal learning, domain adaptation, and explainability**—these would be particularly relevant. I’m treating “recent” as publications and events available by **May 2023**.

## Publications and surveys

### Explainable AI and trustworthy medical imaging

1. **van der Velden et al. (2022)**  
   *Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in deep learning-based medical image analysis.*  
   **Medical Image Analysis, 79, 102470.**  
   A strong field-specific review covering saliency maps, feature attribution, counterfactual explanations, concept-based methods, and evaluation issues.

2. **Ghassemi, Oakden-Rayner & Beam (2021)**  
   *The false hope of current approaches to explainable artificial intelligence in health care.*  
   **The Lancet Digital Health, 3(11), e745–e750.**  
   Important for critically assessing whether visual explanations are clinically meaningful or merely persuasive.

3. **Amann et al. (2020)**  
   *Explainability for artificial intelligence in healthcare: a multidisciplinary perspective.*  
   **BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, 20, 310.**  
   Useful for connecting technical explanations with clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements.

4. **Adebayo et al. (2018)**  
   *Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps.*  
   **NeurIPS.**  
   Not medical-imaging-specific, but essential when evaluating Grad-CAM, integrated gradients, occlusion maps, and related methods.

5. **Rudin (2019)**  
   *Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead.*  
   **Nature Machine Intelligence, 1, 206–215.**  
   A useful counterpoint to post-hoc explanation methods, particularly for clinical decision support.

For your work, I would pay special attention to papers that evaluate explanations using **annotation agreement, perturbation tests, deletion/insertion metrics, localization, robustness, and clinician studies**, rather than only showing heatmaps.

### Segmentation and foundation-model developments

6. **Isensee et al. (2021)**  
   *nnU-Net: a self-configuring method for deep learning-based biomedical image segmentation.*  
   **Nature Methods, 18, 203–211.**  
   Still an important baseline and methodology reference for robust medical segmentation experiments.

7. **Hatamizadeh et al. (2022)**  
   *Swin UNETR: Swin Transformers for Semantic Segmentation of Brain Tumors in MRI Images.*  
   **Proceedings of MICCAI 2022.**  
   Relevant if you are exploring transformer-based architectures and 3D volumetric segmentation.

8. **Ma et al. (2023)**  
   *Segment Anything in Medical Images*—the **MedSAM** preprint.  
   This is worth following for promptable segmentation, transfer learning, and large-scale pretraining, although the work was still developing rapidly in 2023.

9. **Kirillov et al. (2023)**  
   *Segment Anything.*  
   **ICCV 2023**—available as a preprint before the conference.  
   The original SAM paper is not medical-specific, but it is highly relevant to studying how general-purpose visual foundation models transfer to medical images.

### Multimodal learning, transfer learning, and domain adaptation

10. **Moor et al. (2023)**  
    *Foundation models for generalist medical artificial intelligence.*  
    **Nature, 616, 259–265.**  
    A useful overview of the movement toward generalist and multimodal medical AI models.

11. **Moor et al. (2023)**  
    *Med-PaLM: A large language model from medical knowledge.*  
    Although focused more on language than imaging, it is useful for understanding the broader foundation-model direction in healthcare.

12. **Zhou et al. (2023)**  
    *A foundation model for generalizable disease detection from retinal images.*  
    **Nature, 622, 156–163**—published later, but the underlying direction was already highly relevant in 2023.  
    For work strictly limited to your cutoff, look for early retinal-imaging foundation-model preprints and multimodal image–text models.

13. **CheXzero: Generalized Zero-Shot Learning for Chest X-ray Classification**  
    A notable line of work using image–text alignment for zero-shot medical-image classification. It is particularly relevant if you are interested in multimodal transfer learning and weak supervision.

Since you’ve been experimenting with beef stew, plant-based dishes, and cashew-based yogurt, a few habits can make slow-cooker results much more consistent:

### For savory recipes
- **Don’t overfill:** Keep the cooker roughly **half to two-thirds full**. Too little can cook unevenly; too much may leave food undercooked.
- **Use the right cut:** Tough, collagen-rich meats—chuck, shoulder, brisket, or chicken thighs—usually work better than lean cuts.
- **Brown meat and sauté aromatics first:** This isn’t required for safety, but it greatly improves flavor and texture.
- **Use less liquid than you would on the stovetop:** Slow cookers lose very little moisture. Usually, liquid should come about **one-third to halfway up** the ingredients, not cover everything.
- **Layer strategically:** Put dense ingredients such as potatoes, carrots, and dried beans toward the bottom, with meat or more delicate vegetables above them.
- **Avoid lifting the lid:** Each opening can significantly extend cooking time. Add quick-cooking ingredients—peas, spinach, herbs, or dairy—near the end.
- **Adjust seasoning at the end:** Long cooking can mute or concentrate salt and spices. Fresh herbs, lemon juice, vinegar, or a little chili can brighten the finished dish.
- **Thicken afterward:** For stew, remove the lid for the final 20–30 minutes on high, or stir in a cornstarch slurry near the end.

### For vegetarian and vegan recipes
- **Don’t add delicate vegetables too early:** Mushrooms, zucchini, greens, and peas can become mushy. Add them during the last 30–60 minutes, depending on size.
- **Soak or precook beans when needed:** Dried kidney beans should be fully boiled before slow cooking because of their natural toxin. Canned beans should go in late so they don’t break down.
- **Expect less browning:** Plant-based ingredients benefit especially from sautéing onions, garlic, mushrooms, or spices before adding them.
- **Add coconut milk or other creamy ingredients late:** This helps prevent splitting and keeps flavors fresher.

### For cashew-based yogurt
- **Blend until completely smooth:** Soak cashews thoroughly, use enough liquid for the blender to circulate, and blend longer than seems necessary.
- **Strain only if needed:** A high-powered blender may produce a smooth enough mixture without straining; a nut-milk bag gives the silkiest texture.
- **Use a thermometer:** For cultured yogurt, heating the mixture to about **180°F/82°C**, then cooling it to around **110°F/43°C** before adding starter helps improve body and consistency.
- **Don’t incubate too hot:** Excessive heat can kill the cultures. Keep the mixture warm and stable rather than actively cooking it.
- **Use a reliable starter:** Choose plain yogurt with live cultures or a yogurt starter, and avoid adding sweeteners or acidic fruit until fermentation is finished.
- **Expect thickeners to help:** A small amount of tapioca starch, agar, or pectin can improve thickness in dairy-free yogurt.

Finally, check your slow cooker’s actual temperature if results are repeatedly inconsistent; older models can run unusually hot or cool. For the best diagnosis, note whether your main problem is **food staying undercooked, turning mushy, drying out, or lacking flavor**.

Since you already carry a portable power bank when traveling, it’s worth first finding out what’s draining your phone so you’re not relying on it constantly:

1. **Check battery usage:** Open **Settings → Battery** and look for apps using an unusually large percentage. Restrict background activity or uninstall apps you rarely use.
2. **Reduce display drain:** Lower brightness, enable auto-brightness, shorten screen timeout, and use a lower refresh rate if your phone offers one. Dark mode can help somewhat, especially on OLED screens.
3. **Improve signal and connectivity:** Weak cellular reception can drain batteries quickly. Use Wi‑Fi when available, disable Bluetooth/GPS/NFC when unnecessary, and consider Airplane Mode in areas with no signal.
4. **Turn on Battery Saver/Low Power Mode:** Use automatic activation at around 20–30%, or enable it during long travel days.
5. **Update and restart:** Install system/app updates and restart the phone occasionally—an app or process may be stuck running.
6. **Check battery health:** If the phone is a few years old, its battery may simply be worn out. Look for a battery-health or diagnostics section in Settings; a significantly degraded battery may need replacement.
7. **Avoid heat:** High temperatures accelerate battery wear. Don’t leave the phone in a hot car or use demanding apps while it’s charging.

If the battery suddenly started draining fast, feels unusually hot, or the phone’s back is swelling, stop using it and have it inspected promptly.

Since you’ve been leaning toward a **Gibson Les Paul**, use the visit to compare a few models—and don’t judge one only by its brand or finish. Focus on how it feels and sounds in your hands.

### What to check in the store

- **Neck comfort:** Play open chords, barre chords, and higher up the neck. Check whether the neck feels too thick, too slim, or tiring.
- **Fretwork:** Run your hand gently along the edges for sharp frets. Play every fret on each string and listen for buzzing, dead notes, or choking during bends.
- **Action and playability:** The strings shouldn’t feel excessively high, but very low action with buzzing may indicate setup issues.
- **Tuning stability:** Tune the guitar, play for several minutes, bend strings, and check whether it stays in tune.
- **Intonation:** Play an open note and its 12th-fret harmonic/fretted equivalent. They should be reasonably close in pitch.
- **Electronics:** Test every pickup position, both volume controls, and both tone controls. Turn knobs slowly and listen for crackling or sudden dropouts.
- **Weight and balance:** Les Paul-style guitars can be fairly heavy. Wear it standing with a strap for a while and check for neck dive or shoulder discomfort.
- **Acoustic resonance:** Play it unplugged briefly. A lively, resonant feel is a good sign, although the amplified sound matters most.
- **Amplified tone:** Use an amp similar to what you normally play through. Try clean, lightly overdriven, and higher-gain settings, including any open-D ideas you’ve been exploring.
- **Coil-splitting, if available:** If you want more tonal flexibility, test the split sound—but make sure you like the guitar’s main humbucker tones first.

### A useful test routine

Bring a few familiar riffs, chords, bends, and fingerpicking patterns. Play the same things on each guitar, rather than relying only on whatever sounds impressive in the store. Also try playing quietly and loudly; some guitars feel great under gain but less inspiring clean.

Before buying, ask whether the price includes a **professional setup**, and inspect the guitar under good lighting for finish damage, loose hardware, or repaired cracks. If two guitars feel equally good, choose the one you naturally keep reaching for.

Since you’ve been reducing sugar, making your own almond-milk creamer, and liked the idea of **lemon-ginger coffee**, here are a few healthier homemade options:

### 1. Vanilla cinnamon almond creamer
- 1 cup unsweetened almond milk  
- 1–2 teaspoons honey or maple syrup  
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract  
- ¼ teaspoon cinnamon  
- Optional: 1 tablespoon unsweetened coconut cream for richness  

Warm gently and whisk or blend until smooth. Start with a small amount of sweetener—you may find the vanilla and cinnamon provide enough flavor.

### 2. Lemon-ginger creamer
- 1 cup unsweetened oat or almond milk  
- 2–3 thin slices fresh ginger  
- A small strip of lemon zest  
- ½ teaspoon vanilla extract  
- Optional: 1 teaspoon honey or maple syrup  

Simmer the milk with the ginger and lemon zest for 3–5 minutes, then strain and cool slightly before adding to coffee. Use lemon zest rather than lemon juice so the coffee doesn’t curdle.

### 3. Date-sweetened creamer
- 1 cup unsweetened almond milk  
- 1 soft Medjool date, pitted  
- ½ teaspoon vanilla  
- Pinch of cinnamon or salt  

Blend until completely smooth. This gives you natural sweetness without adding refined sugar, though it still contributes sugar and calories.

### 4. Creamy cashew creamer
- ½ cup soaked raw cashews  
- ¾ cup water  
- 1 teaspoon vanilla  
- Pinch of cinnamon  
- Optional: ½ teaspoon maple syrup  

Blend until silky smooth. It’s especially good in strong coffee and can be stored in the refrigerator for about 3–4 days.

**Tip:** For a more concentrated creamer, use half the water or add a tablespoon of unsweetened coconut milk. Store homemade creamer in a sealed jar, shake before using, and refrigerate.

Given that you want **centralized backup for your laptop and phone**, plus strong security features such as encryption and access controls, I’d lean toward **buying a NAS now rather than waiting**—provided you have a clear storage need and budget.

### Buy now if:
- Your current external-drive backup is inconvenient or incomplete.
- You want automatic backups, file syncing, and centralized photo storage.
- You’re comfortable setting it up securely: automatic updates, strong passwords, 2FA, and no unnecessary internet exposure.
- You can buy NAS-rated drives separately and keep an additional backup elsewhere.

A NAS is especially useful for your situation because it can make regular backups much easier—but remember that **a NAS alone is not a complete backup strategy**. Important files should also exist on an external drive or cloud service, ideally following the 3-2-1 approach.

### Consider waiting if:
- Your current storage and backup system works reliably.
- You’re unsure whether you need two or four drive bays.
- You’re waiting for a specific sale or for a newer model with features you actually need.
- You expect your storage needs to change soon—for example, adding several computers, storing lots of video, or running virtual machines.

### What I’d choose for you
Since you were looking at beginner-friendly Synology and QNAP options and care about security:

- **2-bay NAS:** Good starting point for backups, documents, and photos. Use mirrored drives for redundancy. This is likely sufficient if you mainly want a personal backup hub.
- **4-bay NAS:** Better if you expect your storage needs to grow, want more flexible RAID options, or plan to store large media libraries.
- **Avoid buying an older entry-level model solely because it is cheap** if its processor, memory, or software-support life is limited. A current model with 2 GB or more RAM and active security updates is generally the better long-term purchase.

My practical recommendation: **buy a current 2-bay model now if you need convenient backups; wait only if you’re uncertain about capacity or are specifically targeting a sale.** Purchase two matching NAS-rated drives, enable snapshots/versioning and 2FA, and maintain a separate backup of irreplaceable data.

Since you’ll be staying near the **Park Hyatt Tokyo in Shinjuku** and already have a **Suica card** and the **TripIt app**, you’re well prepared. A few tips should make getting around much less stressful:

### 1. Use Suica for most local travel
- Tap in and out on JR trains, subways, and many buses.
- Keep a balance of roughly **¥2,000–¥3,000** so you don’t have to recharge constantly.
- Suica generally doesn’t cover limited-express or reserved-seat supplements, such as some trains to **Nikko**—you may need a separate ticket or reservation.

### 2. Know the difference between train systems
Tokyo has several operators:
- **JR East** — useful for Shinjuku, Shibuya, Tokyo Station, and many airport connections.
- **Tokyo Metro** and **Toei Subway** — useful for areas such as Tsukiji, Asakusa, and Tokyo Tower.

Your Suica works across them, but transfers can involve changing stations or walking through large corridors.

### 3. Allow extra time in Shinjuku
Shinjuku Station is huge and confusing even for locals. For your first few trips:
- Follow signs for the specific **line and exit number**, not just “Shinjuku.”
- Give yourself **15–20 extra minutes**.
- The **West Exit** is likely the most useful area for the Park Hyatt, but confirm the hotel’s current shuttle or walking directions before leaving.

### 4. Use a navigation app
Google Maps is especially helpful in Tokyo because it shows:
- The correct station entrance and exit
- The train platform
- Which car is best for transfers
- Fare and departure times

Search for the exact destination—for example, “Tsukiji Outer Market” rather than simply “Tsukiji”—and save your hotel as your return point.

### 5. Plan your major trips simply
- **Narita Airport to Shinjuku:** Choose one direct option rather than mixing multiple trains. The Narita Express is comfortable and straightforward, though it requires a separate reserved ticket.
- **Tsukiji:** Take the subway and follow signs for **Tsukijishijo** or **Tsukiji**, depending on the route. The market is walkable from either area.
- **Tokyo Tower:** **Akabanebashi Station** is usually a convenient subway stop.
- **Nikko:** Check whether your guided tour includes the train tickets; if not, reserve any required limited-express seat in advance.

### 6. Build in a “wrong turn” buffer
Tokyo trains are punctual, but stations can be sprawling. Avoid scheduling attractions back-to-back. Arriving **10–15 minutes early** is sensible, especially for your Nikko tour meeting point.

### 7. Small habits that help
- Stand on the left or right side of escalators according to local custom, and avoid blocking passageways.
- Keep your phone’s battery charged; a portable charger is useful.
- Carry some cash—small restaurants and older shops may not accept cards.
- If you get lost, go to a station information desk or ask: **“Sumimasen, eki wa doko desu ka?”** (“Excuse me, where is the station?”)
- Save your hotel name and address in Japanese on your phone for taxis or assistance.

For your first day, consider taking one easy practice trip from the hotel to a nearby destination, then returning before tackling Tsukiji or Tokyo Tower. Using **TripIt for your schedule** and **Google Maps for real-time navigation** should give you a reliable backup at every step.
